question: Manipulation check before the payoff study: do the conflict-handling instructions from the coding studies, reworded for a price negotiation, change how an LLM player negotiates? Measured on NegotiationArena's buy-sell game by the labeled style, the concession curve and the share of the surplus the instructed player gets.

source.game: buy_sell: one object X; the seller knows its cost, the buyer its limit; alternating proposals in ZUP, at most 4 own proposals each, ACCEPT or REJECT ends the game (iterations 10)

instances.note: 20 instances shared by every condition; the instructed (focal) player is the seller in even instances and the buyer in odd ones; the other player gets the game's plain prompt

payoff_statement.seller: Your payoff is the price you receive minus your production cost of {cost} ZUP if the trade happens, and 0 if it does not. Try to get as high a payoff as you can.
payoff_statement.buyer: Your payoff is your limit of {limit} ZUP minus the price you pay if the trade happens, and 0 if it does not. Try to get as high a payoff as you can.
payoff_statement.note: appended to each player's role line; NegotiationArena's own prompt states only the cost or limit, and with it the seller opened at cost and the buyer accepted at once in the smoke test

instruction_prefix: [Guidance] You and the other player want different things from this trade: you want a price that is good for your side, they want one that is good for theirs.

neutral.instruction: Handle this in whatever way you think best.
neutral.note: control: draws the same attention to the conflict of interest as the style conditions

competing.instruction: Handle it like this: hold out for the price your side needs. Tell the other player what you need and ask them to come to you. Do not give ground for their sake.

collaborating.instruction: Handle it like this: work out with the other player a deal that is good for both of you. Ask what they need and why, say what you need, and look for a price and terms you can both fully accept.

compromising.instruction: Handle it like this: settle quickly on a middle ground you can both accept. Meet the other player halfway, give up a little if needed, and do not drag the negotiation out.

accommodating.instruction: Handle it like this: put the other player's needs first. Ask what they need, accept a price that works for them, and give ground whenever that helps them.

avoiding.instruction: Handle it like this: do not haggle over the price. Keep messages to a minimum, make at most one proposal of your own, and if the other player does not accept it, end the negotiation rather than argue.

predictions.manipulation: each style condition moves the focal player's labeled style toward its target more often than neutral does; the coding studies induced collaborating, compromising and avoiding but not competing or accommodating
predictions.payoff: competing raises the focal player's share of the surplus and lowers the deal rate; accommodating lowers the focal share; avoiding lowers the deal rate and the number of messages; collaborating and compromising stay near neutral on share
predictions.decision: a condition counts as induced when its target style is labeled in more games than under neutral (paired by instance) and the concession curve differs in the predicted direction; conditions that are not induced need behavioural rules instead of style sentences before the main study

labeler.input: the public moves and messages in order; not the valuations, the private reasoning, the instruction or the outcome

status: written 2026-11-20 before any game was played
